result: In C. reinhardtii, microtubules and associated proteins are added simultaneously during flagellar growth. The axoneme in growing C. reinhardtii flagellar tips displayed regular spacing of doublet microtubules with associated structural proteins present all the way to the tip.
evaluation: Claims C6, C57, and C125 are well-supported by electron tomography data showing organized flagellar tips with associated proteins present (Figures 1F,G, 2H-J). The data consistently demonstrate simultaneous assembly of microtubules and structural proteins in C. reinhardtii.

result: In T. brucei long flagella, disorganized arrays of microtubules are arranged into the axoneme structure by the later addition of preformed protein complexes. Growing long T. brucei flagellar tips showed disorganized doublet microtubules that lose their circular arrangement within ~150 nm of the tip, with associated complexes not visible at the tip but appearing ~0.5 μm proximally.
evaluation: Claims C7, C58-C69, and C124 are strongly supported by electron tomography data (Figures 1E, 2A-G, 7C) showing disorganized microtubule arrays at growing tips and the spatial progression of protein complex incorporation. The small sample size (n=10, Table 1) is acknowledged but the consistent observations across samples support the conclusion.

result: Post assembly, the T. brucei transition zone alters structure and its association with the central pair loosens. The basal plate changes from two stacked electron-dense rings (~30 nm thick) in new flagella to a diffuse electron dense mass (up to 90 nm thick) in old flagella, with central pair minus ends showing loosened anchoring in mature flagella.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C96-C103 are well-supported by electron tomography data from five cells showing structural changes over the cell cycle (Figure 5). The progression from capped to open central pair ends and the structural transformation of the basal plate are clearly documented with quantitative measurements.

result: In growing long T. brucei flagella, the central pair lagged behind doublet microtubules by ~50 nm (p<0.01), while in C. reinhardtii, the central pair extended ~50 nm beyond most doublet microtubules (p<0.01).
evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 are supported by statistical analysis of electron tomography data (Figure 3B, Table 3) with significant p-values (<0.01). The measurements are quantitative and the statistical tests are appropriate for comparing microtubule extensions within axonemes.

result: The singlet region is not found in either species examined. All microtubule tips were found within a small distance from the tip (maximum 230 nm in C. reinhardtii, 125 nm in T. brucei), contradicting previously published observations of a ~1 μm singlet region.
evaluation: Claims C86, C78, and C147 are supported by electron tomography measurements (Table 2, Figure 3A) showing all microtubule ends within 230 nm of the membrane. The comparison with chemically fixed samples (C82-C85) provides evidence that previous observations may have been artifacts of fixation methods.

result: There are multiple ways to form a flagellum. The two species examined display two different assembly pathways, with differences in establishing axoneme organization during microtubule elongation and maturation of the proximal region during the cell cycle.
evaluation: Claims C10, C87, C121, C140-C141, and C163 represent the main conclusion drawn from the comparative electron tomography data. The evidence from multiple results showing distinct assembly mechanisms in T. brucei versus C. reinhardtii strongly supports this overarching conclusion.

result: There is no difference in growth in short T. brucei and C. reinhardtii flagella, but differences were detected in short versus long growing flagellar tips in T. brucei.
evaluation: Claims C123 and C157 are supported by comparative electron tomography data (Figures 1C,D,F,G) showing similar organized structures in short flagella of both species, while long T. brucei flagella show distinct disorganized growth patterns. The length-dependent differences are well-documented.

result: The C. reinhardtii central cylinder structure merely grows lengthwise during flagellar maturation, maintaining consistent proportions (upper basket 60±5%, lower basket 28±5% of total thickness). The structural alterations in the region of central pair nucleation during flagellar maturation in T. brucei are not conserved between the two species.
evaluation: Claims C104-C114 are supported by electron tomography data from nine transition zones (Figure 6) showing consistent proportions despite varying flagellar lengths. The measurements are quantitative and demonstrate a fundamentally different maturation pattern compared to T. brucei.

result: In growing long T. brucei flagellum, central pair projections were found ~0.5 μm from the distal tip, radial spokes were incorporated at ~0.25 μm where the axoneme regained normal circular arrangement, and the paraflagellar rod was added last at ~800 nm from the tip.
evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by electron tomography data showing the spatial progression of component assembly (Figure 7C). The measurements provide a clear timeline of assembly events, confirming the crucial role of radial spokes in organizing the circular arrangement.

result: In all cases except growing long T. brucei flagella, flagellar extension does not require close contact between doublet microtubules and flagellar membrane. Only in disorganized growing long T. brucei flagella did doublet microtubules sometimes touch the flagellar membrane.
evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by quantitative measurements of microtubule-to-membrane distances (Table 2, Figure 3A). The data show consistent spacing in most conditions, with only growing long T. brucei flagella showing direct membrane contact.

result: The A-tubule commonly extended furthest within doublet microtubules, but the extension did not protrude more than 10-20 nm beyond its partner tubule, with no samples showing significant differences between A- and B-tubule extension.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by electron tomography data and statistical analysis (Figure 3C,D; Table 3). The measurements are quantitative and the lack of significant differences is properly tested statistically.

result: Chemical fixation caused artifacts in flagellar tip structure. In chemically fixed cells, microtubule ends were spread over larger distances (up to 350 nm) compared to high pressure frozen samples (maximum 125 nm), and the distal flagellar arrangements previously published in C. reinhardtii tips were likely disturbed by chemical fixation.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by comparative electron tomography data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing systematic differences between fixation methods. This provides important methodological insight explaining discrepancies with prior literature.

result: The ends of doublet microtubules and central pair did not significantly differ in their extension in most samples.
evaluation: Claim C75 is supported by statistical analysis (Figure 3B, Table 3) showing no significant differences in most samples. The exceptions (C76, C77) are separately documented with significant p-values.

result: Most microtubule ends appeared flared, with some caps visible on central pair microtubules. Filamentous material was seen between structures, and electron densities were visible in mature flagella, but results are inconclusive about microtubule-membrane linkages in growing axonemes.
evaluation: Claims C89-C95 describe observations of microtubule end structures and potential membrane linkages (Figure 4). While some structures are documented, the authors explicitly state results are inconclusive for growing axonemes (C95), and the evidence for clear structural links is limited.

result: No obvious central pair cap was found as previously described, though evidence for filamentous proteins extending into the central pair lumen was seen. The central pair extended only ~50 nm further than doublet microtubules, not ~400 nm as previously published.
evaluation: Claims C148-C150 are supported by electron tomography data (Figure 4) showing differences from previously published structures. The measurements contradict prior literature but are consistent with the high-quality preservation methods used in this study.

result: Speculation about mechanisms: The presence of anchorage in C. reinhardtii could provide structural clues holding the axoneme in a close-to-circular arrangement, facilitating incorporation of associated proteins. The absence of axonemal components at long growing T. brucei tips might indicate IFT is rate limiting.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 and C159-C160 are explicitly speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While these hypotheses are reasonable interpretations of the data, they require additional experimental validation and are not directly tested in this study.

result: The structural differences observed are not caused by different flagellar growth rates. C. reinhardtii flagella grow at 12-24 μm/hr initially (declining to 9 μm/hr), while T. brucei flagella grow at a constant ~4 μm/hr.
evaluation: Claims C130-C132 are supported by citations to published literature on growth rates. The comparison appropriately rules out growth rate as an explanation for the observed structural differences, though C131 involves inference from PFR growth rate data.

result: Methodological considerations: Deflagellation was not used to create regenerating flagella in C. reinhardtii, as regrowth after deflagellation might differ from natural post-mitotic regrowth. Pre-mitotic reabsorption likely allows storage of flagellar proteins, and different deflagellation methods affect the basal plate differently.
evaluation: Claims C142, C144-C146 are supported by methodological statements and citations. Claim C143 is speculative but reasonable. These claims provide important context for interpreting the results and comparing with prior literature using different methods.

result: Background on ciliopathies: Defects in flagella growth are related to human diseases including skeletal deformations, polycystic kidney disease, infertility, situs invertus, blindness, obesity, and cancer. The ultrastructural pathology of many ciliopathies remains unknown.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C16-C25 provide established background knowledge supported by citations to published literature. These claims establish the medical relevance and motivation for the study but are not novel findings of this work.

result: Background on flagellar structure and function: Established knowledge about axoneme composition, structure, assembly, and function including microtubule organization, dynein arms, radial spokes, intraflagellar transport, and previously characterized flagellar tip structures.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C12-C15, C26-C56 provide established background knowledge supported by citations to published literature. These claims establish the scientific context but are not novel findings of this work.

result: Biological context for differences: In T. brucei, the new flagellum is not necessary for cell motility since the old flagellum is present, while in C. reinhardtii, both flagella have been shed before mitosis making rapid functional establishment important. Additional differences include beat form, presence of paraflagellar rod, and central pair rotation.
evaluation: Claims C133-C139 provide biological context supported by established knowledge and citations. These claims help explain why different assembly mechanisms might have evolved in the two species, though they are interpretive rather than direct findings.

result: Broader implications: Species-specific structural knowledge is critical before evaluating flagellar defects. The internal environments of flagella of different species may be more different than presently assumed. Understanding ciliogenesis is crucial for understanding flagellar structure, function, and ciliopathies.
evaluation: Claims C11, C151-C152, and C162 represent broader implications and conclusions drawn from the findings. While C151-C152 are somewhat speculative, C11 and C162 are well-supported conclusions about the importance of the work for understanding ciliopathies.

result: Length-dependent growth in C. reinhardtii: Flagellar growth rates are length dependent with shorter flagella growing faster, forming the basis of the balance-point model. The modes of assembly in short and long post-mitotic C. reinhardtii tips do not differ beyond central pair extension.
evaluation: Claims C153-C155 are supported by citations to published literature. Claim C156 is a conclusion drawn from the electron tomography data showing similar assembly modes in short and long C. reinhardtii flagella, consistent with the length-dependent growth model.

result: Prior work on membrane linkages and IFT: Dentler (1980) showed membrane linkages in growing C. reinhardtii axonemes, while Woolley et al. (2006) failed to see them in growing Leishmania major flagella. IFT traffic in T. brucei differs considerably from C. reinhardtii.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 and C161 cite prior published work that provides context for interpreting the current findings. These are accurate representations of prior literature used to support the discussion.
